entry.title: Emergency Session Cleanup — 9.9MB 0.18MB
entry.summary:
Emergency Session Cleanup — 9.9MB → 0.18MB
Session storage ballooned to 9.9MB, causing severe gateway response delays. Identified and cleaned stale, orphaned, and duplicate sessions. Result: 9.9MB → 0.18MB (98% reduction), response speed normalized. Root cause: no automatic session expiration was configured. Fix: set 7-day TTL and added periodic cleanup to cron. Memory leaks happen in data stores, not just processes.

entry.title: Building Reliable Systems in Elixir: The "Let It Crash" Philosophy
entry.summary: Software systems fail. A background job crashes, a request throws an error, or a small bug causes part of an application to stop working. Often, a single failure can affect the entire system. Most programming languages try to prevent crashes by handling errors everywhere using checks, conditionals, and exceptions to keep the program running. Elixir takes a different approach. Instead of trying to stop every failure, Elixir assumes that crashes will happen and focuses on ensuring the system can recover quickly when they do. Elixir runs on the BEAM, a runtime originally designed for systems that must stay online even when parts fail. Rather than letting one error bring everything down, BEAM isolates problems and keeps the rest of the system running. In this article, we’ll explore how Elixi…

entry.title: When a Robot Demo Turns Into a PR Crisis: Lessons from an AI Summit
entry.summary: Technology events are meant to celebrate innovation. Recently, during an AI summit in Delhi, a quadruped robot was showcased at a university pavilion. Later, it was identified as a commercially available robot model that can be purchased online. After social media discussions and media attention, the university released an official press statement. They clarified that a representative at the booth was not fully aware of the technical origin of the product and unintentionally gave incorrect information. This situation quickly became a trending topic. But beyond politics and noise, there are important lessons for the tech community. 1. Using Imported Hardware Is Normal In the AI and robotics world, it is common to use existing hardware platforms. AI models Control systems Computer vision layers Custom software stacks Innovation does not always mean building hardware from scratch. 2.Communication Matters as Much as Code Engineers focus on building systems. If a product is: Imported hardware Customized locally Or used as a demo platform It must be explained clearly. One small misstatement can damage credibility. 3. Social Media Amplifies Everything Today, every tech event is recorded. This means institutions must: Train representatives Prepare clear technical explanations Avoid exaggerated claims Transparency builds trust. Final Thought As developers and tech enthusiasts, we should remember: Building technology is important. Innovation grows stronger when it is honest, transparent, and clearly communicated.
